z-m-37-01.title: How should we say 'broke the rule'?
z-m-37-01.topic: The negation of a condition joined by 'and' (gym use rules)
z-m-37-01.goal: Use concrete student cases to examine what it means to break 'p and q', and find and fix the line that went wrong in a solution that wrote the negation incorrectly.
z-m-37-01.material: The school gym has this rule posted: 'To enter the gym, you must wear indoor shoes and wear a name tag.' Let p be 'wore indoor shoes' and q be 'wore a name tag'. The rule means you must satisfy both 'p and q'. The cases where the rule is broken are the cases that are not 'p and q'. Jiho solved for these 'rule-breaking cases' as below.
z-m-37-01.thinking.0: Finding the line where the error first occurred
z-m-37-01.thinking.1: Checking the meaning of a negation with concrete cases
z-m-37-01.thinking.2: Explaining the corrected expression with cases
z-m-37-01.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-01.prereq.1: The meaning of propositions and conditions, the meaning of '~p' (not p) and of 'and' and 'or', and the meaning of a truth set
z-m-37-01.s.s1.prompt: Which is the first line in Jiho's solution that goes wrong? Press a line to choose it.
z-m-37-01.s.s1.hint.0: Check in order whether each line follows directly from the line before.
z-m-37-01.s.s1.line.0: p is 'wore indoor shoes' and q is 'wore a name tag', and the rule is 'p and q'.
z-m-37-01.s.s1.line.1: The cases that break the rule are the cases that are not 'p and q', that is, ~(p and q).
z-m-37-01.s.s1.line.2: A negation can be put on each part, so ~(p and q) is '~p and ~q'.
z-m-37-01.s.s1.line.3: Therefore a student who did not wear indoor shoes but wore a name tag has not broken the rule.
z-m-37-01.s.s1.explain: It first goes wrong at line 3. Breaking 'you must do both' is not only 'the case where neither is done' but 'the case where at least one of the two is not done'. Line 4 is the wrong result of line 3. Lines 1 and 2 are right.
z-m-37-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the students who cannot enter the gym under the rule (who break the rule).
z-m-37-01.s.s2.hint.0: Put the four kinds of students in a table and write 'indoor shoes yes/no, name tag yes/no' for each.
z-m-37-01.s.s2.hint.1: Decide one at a time whether each kind satisfies 'wore indoor shoes and wore a name tag'.
z-m-37-01.s.s2.o.a: A student who wore indoor shoes and also wore a name tag
z-m-37-01.s.s2.r.a: This student has both conditions. Check whether you put a student who kept the rule among those who broke it.
z-m-37-01.s.s2.o.b: A student who did not wear indoor shoes but wore a name tag
z-m-37-01.s.s2.o.c: A student who wore indoor shoes but did not wear a name tag
z-m-37-01.s.s2.o.d: A student who neither wore indoor shoes nor wore a name tag
z-m-37-01.s.s2.explain: There are three kinds of students who break the rule. The rule 'you must do both' is broken if even one of the two is missing.
z-m-37-01.s.s3.prompt: Correct it and tell Jiho. Explain how to write '~(p and q)' in everyday words and why the 'and' changes, using one kind of student above as an example.
z-m-37-01.s.s3.hint.0: Look at what is missing in common from the students you chose above as 'cannot enter'.
z-m-37-01.s.s3.hint.1: Choose one kind of student and write in a sentence which of p and q that student does not satisfy.
z-m-37-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: A student who wore indoor shoes but has no name tag ...
z-m-37-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the corrected expression I wrote match the meaning 'at least one of the two is not satisfied'?
z-m-37-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: In the example I gave, did I say clearly which condition was missing?
z-m-37-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I explain why the misunderstanding 'only students who did neither break the rule' arises?
z-m-37-01.s.s3.model.0: A violation is the case where they 'did not wear indoor shoes or did not wear a name tag'. A student who wore indoor shoes and only lacks a name tag also failed to keep 'have both', so it is a violation, and ~p or ~q is right.
z-m-37-01.s.s3.model.1: ~(p and q) is '~p or ~q'. A student who did not wear indoor shoes or one who did not wear a name tag, missing just one is a violation, and a student missing both is only one of those cases.

z-m-37-02.title: How many counterexamples are there to 'x² is always greater than x'?
z-m-37-02.topic: The negation of a proposition that begins 'for every real number x', and the range of counterexamples
z-m-37-02.goal: Write exactly the negation of a universal proposition ('every ...'), build several values that are counterexamples, and sum up the range of counterexamples in words.
z-m-37-02.material: Call the following proposition P. P: 'For every real number x, x² > x.' (x² > x is read 'the square of x is greater than x'.) Think over all real numbers.
z-m-37-02.thinking.2: Saying why even one counterexample is enough
z-m-37-02.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-02.prereq.1: The meaning of 'every' and 'some' (existence), and basic quadratic inequalities to the extent of handling the solution of the inequality x²≤x
z-m-37-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most suitable negation of P.
z-m-37-02.s.s1.hint.0: Find whether there are two places in the sentence that change: the opening phrase (every/some) and the inequality sign at the end.
z-m-37-02.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether x² > x is true for x=0 and x=1.
z-m-37-02.s.s1.o.a: For every real number x, x² ≤ x
z-m-37-02.s.s1.r.a: You kept 'every' as it is and changed only the inequality sign. Think about how 'every' changes when you negate.
z-m-37-02.s.s1.o.b: For some real number x, x² ≤ x
z-m-37-02.s.s1.r.b: You changed 'every' to 'some' and also handled the negation of the inequality sign correctly (the opposite of > is ≤).
z-m-37-02.s.s1.o.c: For some real number x, x² < x
z-m-37-02.s.s1.r.c: You changed 'every' well, but wrote < as the opposite of >. Think about where to put the case x²=x.
z-m-37-02.s.s1.o.d: There is no real number x with x² > x
z-m-37-02.s.s1.r.d: You read the negation of 'every' as 'none'. This is a much stronger claim than a negation.
z-m-37-02.s.s1.explain: The negation of 'for every x, p(x)' is 'for some x, ~p(x)'. The negation of x² > x is x² ≤ x (including the equal case).
z-m-37-02.s.s2.prompt: Make three different real numbers x that satisfy the negation of P, that is, counterexamples to P. (Decimals are fine.)
z-m-37-02.s.s2.hint.0: Put in a few values of x between 0 and 1 and see whether squaring x makes it bigger or smaller than x.
z-m-37-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put in 0 and 1 separately and compare.
z-m-37-02.s.s2.hint.2: Put in a negative number and a number greater than 1, one each, and compare the result for P.
z-m-37-02.s.s2.ok.c1: x² is at most x. It is a counterexample to P.
z-m-37-02.s.s2.fail.c1: x² is greater than x. This is a value for which P actually holds. Compare the square with x itself.
z-m-37-02.s.s2.explain: The x that satisfy x² ≤ x are all the numbers from 0 to 1. For example, 0 gives 0 ≤ 0, 1 gives 1 ≤ 1, and 0.5 gives 0.25 ≤ 0.5. There are infinitely many counterexamples, but even one makes P false.
z-m-37-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Write in one sentence what range of numbers the counterexamples you found are in, and write why you can say 'P is false' even if there is only one counterexample.
z-m-37-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Look at where the three values you made are on a number line.
z-m-37-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about how many values are needed to break the word 'every'.
z-m-37-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: The counterexamples are numbers between ..., and ...
z-m-37-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did I check separately whether 0 and 1 are in the range I gave?
z-m-37-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did I use the number of counterexamples needed to break 'every' as my reason?
z-m-37-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Are my three values really inside that range?
z-m-37-02.s.s2.because.model.0: The counterexamples are numbers from 0 to 1. It said 'it holds for every x', so if even one x doesn't fit, the proposition is false.
z-m-37-02.s.s2.because.model.1: The x between 0 and 1 (including 0 and 1) are counterexamples. Even one counterexample breaks 'every', so it is enough.

z-m-37-03.title: If you split 'A−(B∪C)', is it the same set?
z-m-37-03.topic: Checking whether a set identity mixing difference and union holds
z-m-37-03.goal: Check whether a set identity is right by considering the eight cases of whether one element belongs or not, find the wrong expression, and pick out the correct ones.
z-m-37-03.material: Minjun claimed this: 'For sets A, B, C, A−(B∪C) = (A−B)∪(A−C) always holds.' (A−B is read 'the difference of A minus B'.) Instead of a picture, you want to check by whether one element x belongs to each of A, B, C (1 if it belongs, 0 if it does not). There are 8 cases, from (A, B, C) = (0,0,0) to (1,1,1).
z-m-37-03.thinking.0: Deciding equality with a membership table
z-m-37-03.thinking.1: Building a membership situation that is a counterexample
z-m-37-03.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-03.prereq.1: The meaning of union, intersection and difference, and the meaning of two sets being equal (each a subset of the other)
z-m-37-03.s.s1.prompt: If you check all 8 cases and want to say the two sets are equal, what must have been confirmed?
z-m-37-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write out the statement that two sets are equal in terms of 'an element x'.
z-m-37-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how the fact that there are only 8 cases helps with the number of checks.
z-m-37-03.s.s1.o.a: It is enough if the results of the two expressions are the same in just one of the 8 cases
z-m-37-03.s.s1.r.a: You tried to say 'always' from the agreement of one case. What about the remaining cases?
z-m-37-03.s.s1.o.b: It is enough if they are the same only in the case where x belongs to neither B nor C
z-m-37-03.s.s1.r.b: You let one special case stand in for all. In other cases they could differ.
z-m-37-03.s.s1.o.c: It is enough if the two sets have the same number of elements
z-m-37-03.s.s1.r.c: Even with the same number, they can be sets made of different elements.
z-m-37-03.s.s1.o.d: The membership of x is the same in both expressions in all 8 cases
z-m-37-03.s.s1.r.d: You turned the meaning of equal sets, 'for every element the membership is the same', into the 8 cases.
z-m-37-03.s.s1.explain: Two sets being equal means that for any element x, if it belongs to one side it belongs to the other. There are only 8 membership situations for x, so they must agree in all 8.
z-m-37-03.s.s2.prompt: Build a membership situation (A, B, C) in which x belongs to A−(B∪C) but not to (A−B)∪(A−C), or the reverse, that is, in which the results of the two expressions differ.
z-m-37-03.s.s2.hint.0: First build the case where x belongs to just one of B and C.
z-m-37-03.s.s2.hint.1: In that case, check whether x belongs to A−(B∪C), and whether it belongs to A−B or A−C.
z-m-37-03.s.s2.ok.c0: a, b, c are all 1 or 0.
z-m-37-03.s.s2.fail.c0: a, b, c can only be 1 if it belongs and 0 if it does not.
z-m-37-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The two expressions give different results for x.
z-m-37-03.s.s2.fail.c1: In this case the results of the two expressions (belongs/does not belong) are the same. Try one where B and C differ.
z-m-37-03.s.s2.explain: If (A,B,C)=(1,1,0), x belongs to B, so it does not belong to A−(B∪C), but it belongs to A−C, so it belongs to (A−B)∪(A−C). The same goes for (1,0,1). So this identity does not hold.
z-m-37-03.s.s3.prompt: You want to fix Minjun's expression so that it always holds. Choose all the expressions that always hold. (Check with the 8 membership cases.)
z-m-37-03.s.s3.hint.0: For each option, compare the membership of the left side and the right side at (1,1,0), (1,0,1), (0,0,1).
z-m-37-03.s.s3.hint.1: Write down one membership situation where the wrong expression shows itself, and compare with the correct options.
z-m-37-03.s.s3.r.a: Check whether the results differ at (1,1,0) or (1,0,1). This expression wrote the rule for swapping intersection and union the wrong way round.
z-m-37-03.s.s3.r.b: You turned the fact that not belonging to B∪C means belonging to neither B nor C into 'and'.
z-m-37-03.s.s3.r.c: If you attach all of C on the right, the elements of C outside A come in too. Check at (0,0,1).
z-m-37-03.s.s3.r.d: You turned the fact that not belonging to B∩C means not belonging to B or not belonging to C into 'or'.
z-m-37-03.s.s3.explain: A−(B∪C) is the elements that belong to A and belong to neither B nor C, so it equals (A−B)∩(A−C). A−(B∩C) is the elements of A that do not belong to B or do not belong to C, so it equals (A−B)∪(A−C). The operation symbols must be swapped.

z-m-37-04.title: Which expression is the same statement written a different way?
z-m-37-04.topic: Picking out the set expressions that mean the same as 'A is a subset of B'
z-m-37-04.goal: Pick out the expressions that mean the same as A⊂B, and show with small examples in which cases the expressions that do not mean the same fail.
z-m-37-04.material: For two sets A, B inside the universal set U, you want to find the expressions that mean the same as 'A⊂B' (A is a subset of B). A^c is 'the complement of A' (the set obtained by removing the elements of A from U). Of the six expressions below, which always mean the same as A⊂B? 'Mean the same' means the expression holds only when A⊂B.
z-m-37-04.thinking.1: Building counterexamples for expressions that are not the same
z-m-37-04.thinking.2: Explaining a misunderstanding of an expression's direction
z-m-37-04.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-04.prereq.1: Subsets; the meaning of union, intersection, difference and complement (thinking within the universal set U); the meaning of two sets being equal
z-m-37-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the expressions that always mean the same as A⊂B.
z-m-37-04.s.s1.hint.0: With the small universal set U={1,2,3}, set A={1}, B={1,2} and check one at a time whether each expression holds.
z-m-37-04.s.s1.hint.1: Using the same method, change to A={1,2}, B={1} and compare whether each expression holds.
z-m-37-04.s.s1.o.a: A∩B=∅ (A and B have no common part)
z-m-37-04.s.s1.r.a: You mixed up 'do not overlap' and 'is contained'. If A is inside B, A and B actually overlap (if A is not the empty set).
z-m-37-04.s.s1.o.b: A−B=∅ (the set A minus B is the empty set)
z-m-37-04.s.s1.r.b: You read it as saying that A has no element outside B.
z-m-37-04.s.s1.o.c: A∪B=A (the union of A and B is A)
z-m-37-04.s.s1.r.c: Check whether you read 'the union becomes A' as A being bigger than B. The direction is the opposite.
z-m-37-04.s.s1.o.d: A^c⊂B^c (the complement of A is a subset of the complement of B)
z-m-37-04.s.s1.r.d: You did not apply the fact that taking complements reverses the direction of inclusion.
z-m-37-04.s.s1.o.e: B^c⊂A^c (the complement of B is a subset of the complement of A)
z-m-37-04.s.s1.r.e: You correctly applied the fact that moving to complements reverses the direction of inclusion.
z-m-37-04.s.s1.o.f: A∩B=A (the common part of A and B is A)
z-m-37-04.s.s1.r.f: You read 'the common part is all of A' as meaning every element of A is also in B.
z-m-37-04.s.s1.explain: The ones that mean the same as A⊂B are A−B=∅, B^c⊂A^c, A∩B=A, and A∪B=B means the same too. A∪B=A means the same as B⊂A, A^c⊂B^c also means the same as B⊂A, and A∩B=∅ means something different, that A and B have no common element.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.prompt: Make an example showing that 'A∪B=A' does not mean the same as A⊂B. The universal set is U={1,2}; decide whether the elements 1 and 2 belong to A and B (1/0), and make three different (A, B) with A⊂B but A∪B≠A.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.hint.0: First decide that every element in A is also in B, and then add one or more elements that are only in B.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the cases where A or B is the empty set also satisfy the condition.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.fail.c0: Only 1 if it belongs and 0 if it does not can be used.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.ok.c1: A⊂B holds. Every element of A is in B.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Some element of A is not in B. A⊂B does not hold.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.ok.c2: There is an element only in B, so A∪B≠A.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.fail.c2: There is no element only in B. Then A∪B=A.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.explain: If A⊂B and A≠B, there is an element only in B, so A∪B=B≠A. Examples: A={1}, B={1,2} or A=∅, B={2}. There are 5 pairs (A,B) in all that meet this condition (the case where A equals B is excluded because then A∪B=A=B).
z-m-37-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Write as sets one example where A⊂B but A∪B=A fails, and write what relationship A and B must have for A∪B=A.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write one example you made in set notation and find A∪B yourself.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write out the statement that A∪B equals A in terms of 'where the elements are'.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did I find A∪B myself for the example I gave?
z-m-37-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did I state the relationship that makes A∪B=A in terms of which of B and A is inside the other?
z-m-37-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Does my example really satisfy A⊂B?
z-m-37-04.s.s2.because.model.0: If A={1}, B={1,2}, then A⊂B but A∪B={1,2}, which is different from A. For A∪B=A, B⊂A must hold.
z-m-37-04.s.s2.because.model.1: If A={2}, B={2,5}, then A∪B={2,5}≠A. A∪B=A means 'every element of B is in A', so the direction is the opposite.

z-m-37-05.title: If 'the application form is a necessary condition', is it enough to just hand in the form?
z-m-37-05.topic: Interpreting necessary and sufficient conditions (participation rules and extra notices)
z-m-37-05.goal: Turn everyday rule sentences into 'if ... then' form, and each time a new notice is given, decide whether to keep or fix your judgment about which condition is necessary or sufficient.
z-m-37-05.material: The announcement for a school club presentation contest is revealed in stages. Let handing in the entry form be p, paying the entry fee be q, and taking part in the contest be r. (This is an imaginary situation.)
z-m-37-05.thinking.1: Keeping or revising judgments as new information arrives
z-m-37-05.thinking.2: Telling necessary conditions from sufficient conditions
z-m-37-05.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-05.prereq.1: The meaning of 'if p then q' and its contrapositive, and the definitions of necessary and sufficient conditions
z-m-37-05.s.s1.prompt: First notice: 'A team that has not handed in the entry form cannot take part in the contest.' Which one is this notice when turned into 'if ... then' form?
z-m-37-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write the notice as 'if ~p then ~r' and look at where p and r are placed.
z-m-37-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think of one team that took part in the contest and work out whether that team handed in the form.
z-m-37-05.s.s1.o.a: If a team hands in the entry form, it takes part in the contest
z-m-37-05.s.s1.r.a: The notice does not say whether every team that handed in the form takes part. Check whether you reversed the direction of the statement.
z-m-37-05.s.s1.o.b: If a team does not hand in the entry form, it takes part in the contest
z-m-37-05.s.s1.r.b: You read the notice as its exact opposite.
z-m-37-05.s.s1.o.c: If a team takes part in the contest, it handed in the entry form
z-m-37-05.s.s1.r.c: You correctly made the contrapositive of 'a team that didn't hand it in can't take part'.
z-m-37-05.s.s1.o.d: If a team takes part in the contest, it did not hand in the entry form
z-m-37-05.s.s1.r.d: You negated even the part that isn't the negation of the conclusion. Think about whether a team that took part handed in the form or not.
z-m-37-05.s.s1.explain: The contrapositive of 'if not p, then not r' is 'if r, then p'. So handing in the entry form (p) is a necessary condition for taking part (r).
z-m-37-05.s.s2.prompt: The notices will be revealed one at a time. Each time, choose your judgment. If you may leave your earlier judgment as it is, you can choose that.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write each notice with arrows, such as 'if p then r', 'if p and q then r', 'there are teams with r even when not q'.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.hint.1: Compare one by one which of the earlier arrows the new notice changes and which it does not.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.0.info: Notice 1 (confirmed above): A team that has not handed in the entry form cannot take part.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.0.ask: What can you say about a team that handed in the entry form?
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.0.after: Handing in the form is a necessary condition, but you can't yet say it is sufficient. It is suitable to hold the judgment back or to leave it as 'there may be other conditions'.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.0.o.a: All teams that handed in the entry form take part
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.0.r.a: You read the entry form as 'all of the conditions for taking part'.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.0.o.b: Among the teams that handed in the entry form, there may be teams that cannot take part
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.0.r.b: You read it as the form being needed but not yet knowing whether it alone is enough.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.0.o.c: Teams that did not hand in the entry form can take part too
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.0.r.c: You read it in a way that conflicts with what the notice says.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.0.o.d: Handing in the entry form has nothing to do with taking part
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.0.r.d: You missed the relationship the notice states.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.1.info: Notice 2 (added): A team that hands in the entry form and pays the entry fee will definitely take part.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.1.ask: Choose what you can say when the two notices are put together.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.1.after: Notice 2 newly tells you 'form ∧ payment ⇒ participation'. 'Participation ⇒ form' from Notice 1 stays the same. Both are correct ways to put it.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.1.o.a: A team that only paid the entry fee and did not hand in the form can also take part
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.1.r.a: You read payment alone as sufficient. Read Notice 1 again.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.1.o.b: Every team that took part in the contest is a team that handed in the entry form
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.1.r.b: This is not the new notice; you summed up what was already settled in Notice 1. You confirmed that it does not change when used together with the new notice.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.1.o.c: A team that handed in the form and also paid takes part
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.1.r.c: You read the new notice as it is and did not miss that the two conditions are needed 'together'.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.1.o.d: All teams that handed in the entry form take part
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.1.r.d: Notice 2 is about teams that also paid. One condition has dropped out.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.2.info: Notice 3 (added): Among the teams that took part, there were also teams that did not pay the entry fee because a judge recommended them.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.2.ask: Now, how can you describe the roles of 'paying the entry fee' and 'handing in the entry form'?
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.2.after: Notice 3 tells you that payment is not necessary (there are teams that took part without paying). Notice 1 about the form has not changed, so you may keep the judgment that it is a necessary condition. Both are reasonable.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.2.o.a: Paying the entry fee is not a necessary condition for taking part
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.2.r.a: You reflected the new information that there are teams that took part without paying the entry fee.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.2.o.b: Paying the entry fee is both a necessary and a sufficient condition for taking part
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.2.r.b: The recommended teams took part without paying. Can it be called necessary?
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.2.o.c: Handing in the entry form is no longer a necessary condition either
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.2.r.c: Notice 3 does not say whether the recommended teams handed in the form. Notice 1 has not changed yet.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.2.o.d: Handing in the entry form is still a necessary condition for taking part
z-m-37-05.s.s2.st.2.r.d: You distinguished that Notice 3 is about payment, and kept the judgment from Notice 1 as it was.
z-m-37-05.s.s2.reflect: Of your earlier judgments, which did you leave as they were after the new notice, and which did you change? When can the same condition be a necessary condition and then stop being one?

z-m-37-06.title: How many subsets are there that 'contain 1 or do not contain 6'?
z-m-37-06.topic: Two ways to count subsets with a condition
z-m-37-06.goal: Split the condition by whether elements are included to count the subsets, and check by comparing 'counting directly' with 'subtracting from the total'.
z-m-37-06.material: Consider subsets X of the universal set U={1,2,3,4,5,6} (the empty set and U itself are also subsets). U has 64 subsets in all.
z-m-37-06.thinking.0: Turning a condition into a choice for each element
z-m-37-06.thinking.1: Counting an 'or' condition in several ways
z-m-37-06.thinking.2: Checking the results against each other
z-m-37-06.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-06.prereq.1: The meaning of a subset, and why a set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets (for each element, choose whether to include it or not)
z-m-37-06.s.s1.prompt: How many subsets X are there in which '1 belongs to X and 6 does not belong to X'?
z-m-37-06.s.s1.hint.0: Count how many elements you have to decide 'include/don't include' for.
z-m-37-06.s.s1.hint.1: Apply the multiplication principle to the remaining elements other than the ones already decided.
z-m-37-06.s.s1.r.a: You read it as deciding whether to include each of the four elements left after taking out the two decided elements.
z-m-37-06.s.s1.r.b: This equals the count when only one element is decided. Count again how many elements are decided.
z-m-37-06.s.s1.r.c: You counted too many decided elements or miscounted the remaining ones. Look again at how many elements can be chosen freely.
z-m-37-06.s.s1.r.d: While counting the cases by multiplication, you got the number of choices wrong. Each element's choice is two options, 'include/don't include'.
z-m-37-06.s.s1.explain: It is already decided that 1 is included and 6 is left out, and the remaining 2, 3, 4, 5 are each free to be included or not, so 2⁴=16.
z-m-37-06.s.s2.prompt: Change the condition. How many subsets X are there in which '1 belongs to X or 6 does not belong to X'? ('Or' includes the case where both are satisfied, not only one of the two.)
z-m-37-06.s.s2.hint.0: First write what the subsets that break the condition look like.
z-m-37-06.s.s2.hint.1: Split into the case where 1 belongs and the case where it does not, and count each.
z-m-37-06.s.s2.r.a: You carried over the answer of the earlier problem. Because of 'or', more X satisfy the condition.
z-m-37-06.s.s2.r.b: This is the same as counting only 'the case where 1 belongs'. The case where 1 does not belong but 6 does not belong either is missing.
z-m-37-06.s.s2.r.c: You treated every subset as satisfying the condition. What about an X that has no 1 and has 6?
z-m-37-06.s.s2.r.d: You handled well the fact that you get the same value whether you see 'or' as subtracting the cases that break it from the total or as splitting the cases and adding.
z-m-37-06.s.s2.explain: Subtracting from the total of 64 the cases that break the condition, that is, the X where '1 does not belong and 6 belongs' (2⁴=16), gives 48. Counting directly gives the same: 32 X where 1 belongs, and 16 X where 1 does not belong and 6 does not belong either, 48 in all.
z-m-37-06.s.s3.prompt: You want to check that you found the answer of s2 in two ways. Choose one of the direct counting method and the subtract-from-the-total method and explain it, and check in one line whether the other method gives the same value.
z-m-37-06.s.s3.hint.0: Choose one method and write down, giving names to them, which cases it counts.
z-m-37-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare with numbers whether the other method also gives the same count.
z-m-37-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: From the total 64, subtract the ... cases, which gives ...
z-m-37-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the two methods, did the kinds of subsets counted overlap or get left out?
z-m-37-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I use in my explanation why powers of 2 appear (each element's choice)?
z-m-37-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I check that the results of the two methods are equal?
z-m-37-06.s.s3.model.0: From the total of 64 subsets, subtract the 16 cases 'no 1 and has 6' and you get 48. Counting directly also gives the same: the 32 with 1 plus the 16 with no 1 and no 6 make 48.
z-m-37-06.s.s3.model.1: When 1 belongs, the remaining 5 elements are free, so 32, and when 1 does not belong, 6 must be left out, so the remaining 4 are chosen, giving 16. The sum is 48, and 64−16 is also 48.

z-m-37-07.title: Is 'I tried a few even numbers and it worked' a proof of this proposition?
z-m-37-07.topic: Proving 'if n² is even, then n is even' to a friend
z-m-37-07.goal: Sort out which direction a friend's check actually proved, choose a correct approach to prove the same proposition, and write it so the friend can understand.
z-m-37-07.material: A proposition P about a natural number n: 'If n² is even, then n is even too.' A friend, Hajun, said this: 'I tried n=2, 4, 6, 8. n² is 4, 16, 36, 64, all even, so P is proved.'
z-m-37-07.thinking.1: Choosing a suitable one among several proof approaches
z-m-37-07.thinking.2: Writing a proof for a friend
z-m-37-07.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-07.prereq.1: Writing even and odd numbers as 2k and 2k+1, reading 'if p then q', and the relationships among such propositions (the link between true and false)
z-m-37-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the reasonable ways to prove P. (Include Hajun's method in your judgment.)
z-m-37-07.s.s1.hint.0: Look at whether the values of n that Hajun put in are all even, and whether the side he checked was the 'hypothesis' or the 'conclusion'.
z-m-37-07.s.s1.hint.1: Write P in 'if ... then' form, and compare which is the hypothesis and which is the conclusion in the statement Hajun checked.
z-m-37-07.s.s1.o.a: Put in a few values where n is even and check whether n² is even
z-m-37-07.s.s1.r.a: Look at the direction checked. This method tests 'if n is even, then n² is even'.
z-m-37-07.s.s1.o.b: Assume n is odd and show that n² is odd
z-m-37-07.s.s1.r.b: This goes in the direction of negating the conclusion and arriving at negating the hypothesis, and uses the fact that this means the same as the original proposition.
z-m-37-07.s.s1.o.c: Prove that if n is even, then n² is even
z-m-37-07.s.s1.r.c: You proved the reverse of P, not P. A reversed proposition being true does not make P true.
z-m-37-07.s.s1.o.d: Assume n² is even but n is odd, and show a contradiction
z-m-37-07.s.s1.r.d: This is a way of assuming the hypothesis and the negation of the conclusion at once to derive a contradiction. You supposed that P is false and worked it out.
z-m-37-07.s.s1.explain: Hajun's check tested 'if n is even, then n² is even' (the converse of P) with a few examples, so it is neither P nor a proof. P is proved by proving its contrapositive ('if n is odd, then n² is odd'), or by showing a contradiction by proof by contradiction.
z-m-37-07.s.s2.prompt: Write the proof of P directly for Hajun. Choose one of the methods you judged reasonable in s1, write an odd number as 2k+1 (k is an integer 0 or greater), and write it in 4 sentences or fewer. It would also be good to add one sentence about what direction Hajun checked.
z-m-37-07.s.s2.hint.0: First write how n can be written if n is odd.
z-m-37-07.s.s2.hint.1: After expanding n², factor out 2 and look at what is left over.
z-m-37-07.s.s2.placeholder: Example: If n is odd, then n=2k+1 and ...
z-m-37-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did my proof exactly show that n² is odd when n is odd (or the contradiction)?
z-m-37-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did I explain why Hajun's check is not a proof, in terms of direction or 'a few examples'?
z-m-37-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did I write it in 4 sentences or fewer so that a friend can read it easily?
z-m-37-07.s.s2.model.0: Contrapositive: if n is odd, then n² is odd too. If n=2k+1, then n²=4k²+4k+1=2(2k²+2k)+1, so it is odd. The contrapositive is true, so P is true too. Hajun checked a few cases of the opposite direction of P.
z-m-37-07.s.s2.model.1: Suppose n² is even but n is odd. If n=2k+1, then n²=2(2k²+2k)+1 is odd, which contradicts its being even. So n is even. Hajun's check was only a few examples.

z-m-37-08.title: We assumed 'the primes are finite' and got a contradiction. Is it really a contradiction?
z-m-37-08.topic: Checking whether the assumption and the contradiction fit together in a proof by contradiction
z-m-37-08.goal: Find the line that goes wrong in a proof that there are infinitely many primes, check a number that is a counterexample, and then rewrite that line.
z-m-37-08.material: This is a student's write-up proving by contradiction that there are infinitely many primes. (p₁, p₂, …, p_k are read 'p one, p two, … p k'. They are the list of all primes.)
z-m-37-08.thinking.0: Checking the logical connections of the proof
z-m-37-08.thinking.1: Testing a claim with concrete numbers
z-m-37-08.thinking.2: Fixing the gap and completing it
z-m-37-08.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-08.prereq.1: Primes, composite numbers, prime factors, and proof by contradiction (negate the conclusion and reach a contradiction)
z-m-37-08.s.s1.prompt: Which is the first line in this proof where a claim is made without grounds?
z-m-37-08.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, check 'does this line follow directly from the line before?'
z-m-37-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare side by side what line 3 tells you and what line 4 says.
z-m-37-08.s.s1.line.0: Suppose the primes are finite, and call all the primes p₁, p₂, …, p_k.
z-m-37-08.s.s1.line.2: Dividing N by any of p₁, …, p_k leaves remainder 1, so N is not divisible by any of them.
z-m-37-08.s.s1.line.3: Therefore N is a prime, and since it is a prime not in the list, this is a contradiction.
z-m-37-08.s.s1.line.4: Therefore there are infinitely many primes.
z-m-37-08.s.s1.explain: It is line 4. Up to line 3, all that was said is that N is not divisible by p₁, …, p_k. That alone does not let you say N is a prime (it could be a composite number).
z-m-37-08.s.s2.prompt: Let's test it. When p₁, …, p_k are the six smallest primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, N = 2×3×5×7×11×13 + 1 = 30031. 30031 = 59 × 509. Choose everything you can learn from this calculation.
z-m-37-08.s.s2.hint.0: Divide 30031 by 59 and check the remainder.
z-m-37-08.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether 59 and 509 are in the list 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13.
z-m-37-08.s.s2.o.a: 30031 is not divisible by any of the first six primes, but it is not a prime
z-m-37-08.s.s2.r.a: You read off at once that the claim of line 3 is right and the claim of line 4 is wrong.
z-m-37-08.s.s2.o.b: It shows that the conclusion itself, that there are infinitely many primes, is false
z-m-37-08.s.s2.r.b: You could not tell apart a line of the proof being wrong from the conclusion being wrong.
z-m-37-08.s.s2.o.c: Even if N is composite, the prime factors 59 and 509 of N are new primes that are not among the first six primes
z-m-37-08.s.s2.r.c: You read off a direction in which the proof can be fixed even if N is not a prime.
z-m-37-08.s.s2.o.d: N is always a prime, so line 4 is right
z-m-37-08.s.s2.r.d: You accepted the claim without ever testing a counterexample. Divide 30031 by 59.
z-m-37-08.s.s2.explain: 30031=59×509 is composite and not divisible by the first six primes, but the claim that N is a prime is wrong. Still, the prime factors 59 and 509 are new primes not in the list. So if you fix line 4 to 'a new prime exists', the proof is complete. Having a counterexample does not make the conclusion itself false.
z-m-37-08.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite line 4. In 2 to 3 sentences, reflecting that N may be a prime or a composite number, write how a prime not in the list appears and so what contradiction arises.
z-m-37-08.s.s3.hint.0: Split into the case where N is a prime and the case where it is not, and write what prime you can find in each.
z-m-37-08.s.s3.hint.1: Compare with the content of line 3 whether that prime could be in the list.
z-m-37-08.s.s3.placeholder: Example: N is either a prime or ...
z-m-37-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I handle both the case where N is a prime and the case where it is not?
z-m-37-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I connect the reason the new prime is not in the list with line 3?
z-m-37-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Does the contradiction meet the assumption that 'the list is all the primes'?
z-m-37-08.s.s3.model.0: N is either a prime or a composite number. If it is a prime, it is a new prime not in the list, and if it is composite, its prime factor is none of p₁…p_k, so it is a new prime. Either way there is a prime not in the list, which contradicts the assumption.
z-m-37-08.s.s3.model.1: Let q be a prime factor of N. Dividing N by a prime in the list leaves remainder 1, so q is different from the numbers in the list. There is a prime q not in the list, which contradicts the assumption that 'the list is all the primes'.

z-m-37-09.title: From three rules, what is 'necessarily true' and what is 'unknown'?
z-m-37-09.topic: Judging a conclusion by chaining several rules (chains of conditions and contrapositives)
z-m-37-09.goal: Chain several 'if ... then' rules and use contrapositives to pick out the conclusions that are necessarily true, and propose what further rule is needed to reach a conclusion.
z-m-37-09.material: Three rules are posted in a school science lab (they are imaginary rules). (가) A student who is not wearing a lab coat cannot take part in the experiment. (나) Every student who received safety goggles has had safety training. (다) Every student who takes part in the experiment receives safety goggles. For one student, think only about whether four facts are true or false: 'is wearing a lab coat', 'received safety goggles', 'has had safety training', 'takes part in the experiment'.
z-m-37-09.thinking.0: Chaining rules to draw a conclusion
z-m-37-09.thinking.2: Admitting the information is insufficient and proposing the information needed
z-m-37-09.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-09.prereq.1: The relationship between 'if p then q' and its contrapositive, and the meaning of necessary and sufficient conditions
z-m-37-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything you can say is necessarily true from (가), (나), (다) alone.
z-m-37-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write each of the three rules in 'if ... then' form and chain them with arrows (→).
z-m-37-09.s.s1.hint.1: Compare each option with the direction of the arrows, and make contrapositives to check if needed.
z-m-37-09.s.s1.o.a: Every student who has had safety training can take part in the experiment
z-m-37-09.s.s1.r.a: You read the direction of (나) backwards. Safety training is a condition for the goggles, not a sufficient condition for the experiment.
z-m-37-09.s.s1.o.b: Every student who is wearing a lab coat received safety goggles
z-m-37-09.s.s1.r.b: You read the direction of (가) backwards. The lab coat is a necessary condition for the experiment.
z-m-37-09.s.s1.o.c: A student who has not had safety training cannot take part in the experiment
z-m-37-09.s.s1.r.c: You correctly used the contrapositive of the conclusion made by chaining (다) and (나).
z-m-37-09.s.s1.o.d: A student who has not received safety goggles cannot take part even with a lab coat
z-m-37-09.s.s1.r.d: You correctly made the contrapositive of (다).
z-m-37-09.s.s1.explain: From (다), experiment→goggles, and from (나), goggles→safety training, so experiment→safety training, and its contrapositive is 'without safety training, no experiment'. The contrapositive of (다) is 'without goggles, no experiment'. a and b reverse the direction of a rule, so they can't be known.
z-m-37-09.s.s2.prompt: Minji has had safety training, is wearing a lab coat, and has received goggles. Judging by the three rules alone, what can you say about whether Minji can take part in the experiment?
z-m-37-09.s.s2.hint.0: For each rule, tell apart whether it says 'you can't without' or 'if you have, you can'.
z-m-37-09.s.s2.hint.1: Imagine whether the rules can stay in force whatever value the taking-part fact has among the four facts.
z-m-37-09.s.s2.o.a: She can take part. Because she has all the necessary conditions
z-m-37-09.s.s2.r.a: You read 'having the necessary conditions' as meaning 'takes part'. Look at which direction the rules speak in.
z-m-37-09.s.s2.o.b: It is not decided. Because the rules only say what is necessary
z-m-37-09.s.s2.r.b: You read off that all three rules say only 'impossible without' and do not say 'possible with'.
z-m-37-09.s.s2.o.c: She cannot take part. Because there is no rule that permits it
z-m-37-09.s.s2.r.c: You treated the absence of a permitting rule as the same as impossibility. Something not being in the rules does not mean it is forbidden.
z-m-37-09.s.s2.explain: All three rules are necessary conditions for taking part. Whether a student who has all the necessary conditions takes part is only decided if there is another rule of the form 'if ..., then they take part'. For now it is not decided.
z-m-37-09.s.s3.hint.0: First tell apart whether the rule you want to propose is 'if ... then they take part' or 'if not ..., then they can't'.
z-m-37-09.s.s3.hint.1: Put the facts Minji has into the condition part of that rule.
z-m-37-09.s.s3.placeholder: Example: We need one more rule that if ..., then they can take part in the experiment. Because ...
z-m-37-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the rule I proposed of the form 'if ... then they take part', a direction not in the current rules?
z-m-37-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I explain that the current rules say only necessary conditions?
z-m-37-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If I add the rule I proposed, is Minji's result actually decided?
z-m-37-09.s.s3.model.0: We need a rule like 'a student who has had safety training, is wearing a lab coat, and received goggles can take part in the experiment'. The current rules only say the cases where they can't, and don't say the conditions under which they can.
z-m-37-09.s.s3.model.1: There has to be a sufficient condition like 'if the teacher permits, they can take part'. The rules above only say a lab coat, goggles, and training are needed, and don't say those alone are enough.

z-m-37-10.title: Are 'every student has a subject they like' and 'there is a subject every student likes' the same statement?
z-m-37-10.topic: Interpreting sentences where 'every' and 'some' overlap (a survey table of favorite subjects)
z-m-37-10.goal: Use a table to check that the meaning changes when the order of 'every' and 'some (there is)' changes, and design yourself how to change the table so that one of the sentences becomes true.
z-m-37-10.material: Students 가, 나, 다 were asked whether they like Korean, math, and English (O means likes, X means does not like). 가: Korean O, math O, English X. 나: Korean X, math O, English O. 다: Korean O, math X, English O. Statement ㄱ: 'Every student has a subject that they like.' Statement ㄴ: 'There is a subject that every student likes.'
z-m-37-10.thinking.0: Deciding whether the two statements are true or false using the table
z-m-37-10.thinking.1: Summing up the difference between the two statements in words
z-m-37-10.thinking.2: Changing the table to design it so a statement becomes true
z-m-37-10.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-10.prereq.1: The meaning of 'every' and 'some', and judging whether a proposition is true or false
z-m-37-10.s.s1.prompt: Look at the table and judge whether ㄱ and ㄴ are true or false.
z-m-37-10.s.s1.hint.0: Check one student at a time whether each has at least one O.
z-m-37-10.s.s1.hint.1: Check one subject at a time whether all three students have O.
z-m-37-10.s.s1.r.a: Check whether you read ㄱ as 'every student likes every subject'.
z-m-37-10.s.s1.r.b: You read the two statements as having the same meaning. Look in the table for whether there is one subject that every student likes.
z-m-37-10.s.s1.explain: ㄱ means each and every student has at least one subject they like, so it is true. ㄴ means there is the same subject that all three students like, but 나 does not like Korean, 다 does not like math, and 가 does not like English, so it is false.
z-m-37-10.s.s2.prompt: Choose the best description of the difference between ㄱ and ㄴ.
z-m-37-10.s.s2.hint.0: Make a situation in the table where ㄴ is true, and check what happens to ㄱ then.
z-m-37-10.s.s2.hint.1: Look for whether the table above has an example where ㄱ is true but ㄴ is false.
z-m-37-10.s.s2.explain: ㄱ allows each student to pick a subject separately (for every student there is some subject), and ㄴ requires one subject to apply to every student (some subject applies to every student). If ㄴ is true, ㄱ is true too, but not the reverse.
z-m-37-10.s.s3.prompt: You want to make ㄴ true by changing as few X cells in the table to O as possible. Write at least one way to do it, saying which student's cell for which subject to change, and write whether ㄱ is still true after the change.
z-m-37-10.s.s3.hint.0: Fix one subject and count how many students have X for that subject.
z-m-37-10.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether changing that student's cell creates a subject that every student likes.

z-m-37-11.title: The rule 'every student 3 m or taller must apply': what happens if there is no such student?
z-m-37-11.topic: The empty set and truth when 'there is no element that fits'
z-m-37-11.goal: When no element at all satisfies the condition, judge from the definition whether a proposition of the form 'every ... is ...' is true or false, and check the doubts that arise from this.
z-m-37-11.material: School rule: 'Every student who is 3 m or taller must hand in an application.' There is not a single student 3 m or taller at this school (this is an imaginary situation). Read this rule as 'if p then q', with p being 'is 3 m or taller' and q being 'hands in an application'.
z-m-37-11.thinking.0: Finding what is needed for it to be false
z-m-37-11.thinking.1: Judging the case where there are no matching elements
z-m-37-11.thinking.2: Checking doubts and revising your judgment
z-m-37-11.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-11.prereq.1: When 'if p then q' is false, and the meaning of truth sets and subsets
z-m-37-11.s.s1.prompt: For 'for every student x, if p then q' to be false, what must exist?
z-m-37-11.s.s1.hint.0: Write in one line each what a student who kept the rule and a student who broke it look like.
z-m-37-11.s.s1.o.a: There is not a single student who is p
z-m-37-11.s.s1.r.a: You read the absence of matching students as the reason for falsity. Think about what kind of student 'breaks the rule' for it to be false.
z-m-37-11.s.s1.o.b: There is a student who is p but not q
z-m-37-11.s.s1.r.b: You pointed exactly to the student who breaks the rule, that is, the counterexample.
z-m-37-11.s.s1.o.c: There is a student who is neither p nor q
z-m-37-11.s.s1.r.c: A student who is not p is not what the rule is talking about.
z-m-37-11.s.s1.o.d: There is not a single student who is q
z-m-37-11.s.s1.r.d: No student satisfying q does not conflict with there being no p. The only problem is a student who is p and does not do q.
z-m-37-11.s.s1.explain: 'If p then q' is false only when there is a student (a counterexample) who satisfies p and does not satisfy q.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.prompt: The information will be revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose your judgment. If your earlier judgment is still reasonable, you may carry it on.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.hint.0: First try to see whether you can find even one student who broke the rule.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.hint.1: Write the rule of each step in the form 'P⊂Q' or 'P⊂ the complement of Q', and check the elements of P one by one.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.0.info: Data 1: At this school there is not a single student 3 m or taller. Rule: Every student 3 m or taller must hand in an application.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.0.ask: Is there a student who broke this rule?
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.0.after: There is none who broke it. For the rule to be false there would have to be a student who is p and not q, but there is no student who is p, so there is no such student.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.0.o.a: There is no student who broke it
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.0.r.a: You applied what you confirmed in s1, that there has to be a student who broke it (a counterexample) for it to be false.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.0.o.b: There are no matching students, so you can't even check whether there is one who broke it
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.0.r.b: You treated 'there is nothing to check' and 'there is no student who broke it' as the same. You have in effect confirmed that there is no such target.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.0.o.c: There is. The violation is that a student 3 m or taller has never handed in an application
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.0.r.c: You read the fact that there are no students as a violation. A violation is a fact about a student.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.0.o.d: The rule is not used on any student, so it is not a rule
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.0.r.d: You judged the force of the rule by whether there is a target. A rule is also made for when targets appear.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.1.info: Data 2: In mathematics this rule is read as P⊂Q. P is the set of students 3 m or taller, and Q is the set of students who handed in an application. Here P is the empty set.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.1.ask: How would you judge the empty set ∅⊂Q?
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.1.after: No element of P is missing from Q, so P⊂Q. ∅⊂Q holds for every set Q.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.1.o.a: It is false. There are no elements, so it can't be called a subset of Q
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.1.r.a: You thought a set has to have elements to be a subset. The meaning of subset is 'every element of P is in Q'.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.1.o.b: It is true. Not a single element of P is outside Q
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.1.r.b: You applied the definition of subset as it is. It is the same as Data 1 in that there is no violation (counterexample).
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.1.o.c: It is true only when Q is the empty set
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.1.r.c: You read it as depending on whether Q has elements. If P has no elements, then whatever Q is, there is no element that broke it.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.1.o.d: It is just a different convention by definition, with no reason
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.1.r.d: It is not a convention but the result of applying the definition. You can state the reason: there is no counterexample.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.2.ask: Say both rules are true. Is this a contradiction?
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.2.after: If there are no matching students, both rules are true. If there is even one matching student, that student either hands in an application or does not, so the two rules cannot both be true at the same time.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.2.o.a: It is a contradiction. One of them must be false
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.2.r.a: You read 'hands in an application' and 'does not hand in' as opposites, so they can't be true together. Think about whether there are matching students.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.2.o.b: It is not a contradiction. There are no matching students, so there is no student who broke either rule
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.2.r.b: You confirmed that there is no student who broke either rule (no counterexample).
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.2.o.c: If even one matching student appears, the two rules can't both be true
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.2.r.c: You pinpointed exactly where the feeling of a contradiction comes from, that is, when a matching student appears.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.2.o.d: Only the first rule is true and the second rule is false
z-m-37-11.s.s2.st.2.r.d: You decided that the second rule is false without looking for a counterexample. Look for whether there is a counterexample.
z-m-37-11.s.s2.reflect: If at first you felt that 'there is nothing to check', how did your judgment change as you thought about the meaning of a counterexample? Why might it feel strange that the two rules are true together?

z-m-37-12.title: Does 'if A⊂B and B⊄C then A⊄C' always hold?
z-m-37-12.topic: Checking whether a conclusion is fixed by inclusion relations (a membership table for three sets)
z-m-37-12.goal: Judge whether a claim about inclusion always holds by building a counterexample with a membership table for two elements, and say whether the given information fixes the relationship between A and C.
z-m-37-12.material: For subsets A, B, C of the universal set U={1, 2}, Seojin said this: 'If A⊂B and B⊄C, then A⊄C.' To test whether this statement always holds, you will use whether the elements 1 and 2 belong to each of A, B, C (1 if it belongs, 0 if not).
z-m-37-12.thinking.0: Sorting out the conditions a counterexample to the claim must meet
z-m-37-12.thinking.1: Building counterexamples yourself with a membership table
z-m-37-12.thinking.2: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-37-12.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-12.prereq.1: The meaning of the subset A⊂B, and the meaning of A⊄B (A is not a subset of B)
z-m-37-12.s.s1.prompt: To show that Seojin's statement does not always hold, what kind of A, B, C must you find?
z-m-37-12.s.s1.hint.0: Write Seojin's statement divided into two parts, the 'hypothesis' and the 'conclusion'.
z-m-37-12.s.s1.hint.1: Pick out which part must be satisfied and which part must be broken.
z-m-37-12.s.s1.o.a: A, B, C with A⊂B and B⊄C and also A⊂C
z-m-37-12.s.s1.r.a: You pointed to an example where the hypothesis is entirely satisfied while the conclusion is false.
z-m-37-12.s.s1.o.b: A, B, C with A⊂B and B⊂C and also A⊄C
z-m-37-12.s.s1.r.b: You read the hypothesis as B⊂C. Seojin's hypothesis is B⊄C.
z-m-37-12.s.s1.o.c: A, B, C with A⊄B and B⊄C and also A⊂C
z-m-37-12.s.s1.r.c: This breaks the first part of the hypothesis, so it has nothing to do with Seojin's statement.
z-m-37-12.s.s1.o.d: A, B, C with A⊂B and B⊄C and also A⊄C
z-m-37-12.s.s1.r.d: You found a case where Seojin's statement holds. To break the statement, you need an example where the conclusion is false.
z-m-37-12.s.s1.explain: A counterexample that breaks 'hypothesis implies conclusion' is a case where the hypothesis is entirely true and the conclusion is false. Here, that is the case with A⊂B, B⊄C, and not A⊄C but A⊂C.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.prompt: Make three different (A, B, C) that break Seojin's statement. Enter as 1 or 0 whether 1 belongs to A, B, C (a1, b1, c1) and whether 2 belongs (a2, b2, c2).
z-m-37-12.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one element of B that is not in C. Think about whether that element also has to be in A.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.hint.1: Let every element of A be in both B and C.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.fail.k0: Only 1 if it belongs and 0 if it does not can be used.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.fail.k1: Not every element of A is in B. A⊂B does not hold.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.ok.k2: B⊄C holds. B has an element that C does not have.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.fail.k2: Every element of B is in C, so B⊄C does not hold.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.ok.k3: A⊂C holds. It is an example that breaks Seojin's conclusion.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.fail.k3: A⊄C holds. This is a case where Seojin's statement holds.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.explain: For example, A=∅, B={2}, C=∅ gives A⊂B, B⊄C, and A⊂C. A={1}, B={1,2}, C={1} works too. There are 9 triples (A, B, C) in all that meet the conditions.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.because.prompt: Write one counterexample you made in the form A=…, B=…, C=…, and write in one sentence why A⊂C can hold even though B⊄C.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the A, B, C you made as sets and point out one element that is in B and not in C.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check whether that element is in A.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: In my example, did I check A⊂B, B⊄C, and A⊂C all directly?
z-m-37-12.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did I use as my reason that the element only in B is not in A?
z-m-37-12.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Do I know that an example where A is the empty set is possible?
z-m-37-12.s.s2.because.model.0: Example: A={1}, B={1,2}, C={1}. A⊂B and B⊄C (2 is not in C), but A⊂C. The element 2 of B that is not in C is not in A, so it has nothing to do with A.
z-m-37-12.s.s2.because.model.1: If A=∅, B={1}, C={2}, then ∅ is a subset of any set, so A⊂C, and B⊄C. This is because the element 1 that is only in B has nothing to do with A.
z-m-37-12.s.s3.prompt: From only the information 'A⊂B and B⊄C', what can you say for certain about the relationship between A and C?
z-m-37-12.s.s3.hint.0: Compare one counterexample you already made with one more example where A⊄C.
z-m-37-12.s.s3.hint.1: Check in both examples whether A⊂B and B⊄C both hold.
z-m-37-12.s.s3.o.a: A is not a subset of C
z-m-37-12.s.s3.r.a: You only thought of examples with A⊄C. In the counterexample you just made, A⊂C.
z-m-37-12.s.s3.o.b: A is a subset of C
z-m-37-12.s.s3.r.b: You only thought of examples with A⊂C. What about an example like A={1}, B={1}, C={2}?
z-m-37-12.s.s3.o.c: A and C have no common element
z-m-37-12.s.s3.r.c: You generalized the shape of one example. Check whether A and C had a common element in the counterexample.
z-m-37-12.s.s3.o.d: It is not decided whether A⊂C
z-m-37-12.s.s3.r.d: You reflected that there are examples where the same hypothesis gives different results.
z-m-37-12.s.s3.explain: For A={1}, B={1,2}, C={1}, A⊂C, and for A={1}, B={1}, C={2}, A⊂B, B⊄C, and A⊄C. Both results are possible from the same information, so it is not decided.

z-m-37-13.title: How are 'both at least 60', 'at least one at least 60', and 'average at least 60' related to each other?
z-m-37-13.topic: Inclusion relations among the sets of students who pass under three pass rules
z-m-37-13.goal: Compare the sets of students who pass under different pass rules to judge inclusion relations, design one more rule, and explain its inclusion relationship with the existing rules.
z-m-37-13.material: In one class you want to decide pass or fail by a math score x and an English score y (each an integer from 0 to 100) (these are imaginary rules). Rule 1: both math and English are at least 60. Rule 2: at least one of math and English is at least 60. Rule 3: the average of the two scores is at least 60 (x+y is at least 120).
z-m-37-13.thinking.0: Knowing that comparison is possible even when you don't know the distribution
z-m-37-13.thinking.1: Showing with counterexamples that the inclusion goes in only one direction
z-m-37-13.prereq.0: The 'H3' of this task is only the difficulty and support level of this production assignment table, and does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns the subject to that grade. It assumes the learner has just learned sets and propositions for the first time in high school.
z-m-37-13.prereq.1: The truth set of a condition and inclusion relations, the meaning of 'and' and 'or', and the meaning of average
z-m-37-13.s.s1.prompt: However the class's scores are given, which rule never passes fewer students than the other two rules?
z-m-37-13.s.s1.hint.1: Check what the average is if both scores are below 60.
z-m-37-13.s.s1.r.a: You thought 'both' is harder. A rule with a stricter passing condition cannot have many passers.
z-m-37-13.s.s1.r.b: You thought the average is in the middle of the two scores and the most moderate. Compare how a student with only one high subject fares under Rule 2 and under Rule 3.
z-m-37-13.s.s1.r.c: If only one subject is at least 60 it passes, so this judgment started from working out which score pairs pass under the other rules.
z-m-37-13.s.s1.o.d: It can only be known once the scores are given
z-m-37-13.s.s1.r.d: You thought comparison is impossible without the score distribution. If there is an inclusion relation between the sets of passers, they can be compared whatever the distribution.
z-m-37-13.s.s1.explain: Passing Rule 1 means also passing Rule 3 and Rule 2, and passing Rule 3 means also passing Rule 2 (if both are below 60, the average is also below 60). So the sets of passers are Rule 1 ⊂ Rule 3 ⊂ Rule 2. Rule 2 screens out the fewest passers.
z-m-37-13.s.s2.prompt: Make two different pairs of (math x, English y) scores for students who pass Rule 3 but do not pass Rule 1. (A pair with only the order swapped is the same example.)
z-m-37-13.s.s2.hint.0: First make a pair of two scores whose average is exactly 60.
z-m-37-13.s.s2.hint.1: Check in that pair whether both scores are at least 60.
z-m-37-13.s.s2.ok.k0: The scores are integers from 0 to 100.
z-m-37-13.s.s2.fail.k0: The scores must be integers from 0 to 100.
z-m-37-13.s.s2.ok.k1: The average is at least 60 (passes Rule 3).
z-m-37-13.s.s2.fail.k1: The average is lower than 60. It does not pass Rule 3.
z-m-37-13.s.s2.ok.k2: The two scores are not both at least 60 (does not pass Rule 1).
z-m-37-13.s.s2.fail.k2: Both scores are at least 60. It passes Rule 1.
z-m-37-13.s.s2.explain: Example: (100, 20) has an average of 60, so it passes Rule 3, but 20 is below 60, so it does not pass Rule 1. (90, 30) and (80, 40) are the same. So the passers of Rule 3 are more than the passers of Rule 1 (the inclusion goes in only one direction).
z-m-37-13.s.s3.prompt: Choose the suitable reason why 'a student who passed Rule 3 definitely passes Rule 2 too' always holds.
z-m-37-13.s.s3.hint.0: Write what range each of the two scores is in for a student who does not pass Rule 2.
z-m-37-13.s.s3.hint.1: Find the largest possible value of x+y in that range and compare it with 120.
z-m-37-13.s.s3.o.a: Because I checked a few examples such as (100, 20)
z-m-37-13.s.s3.r.a: You said 'always' just from checking examples. A few examples are different from all cases.
z-m-37-13.s.s3.o.b: Because if the average is at least 60, both scores must be at least 60
z-m-37-13.s.s3.r.b: This conflicts with the example in s2. Even if the average is 60, one score can be 20.
z-m-37-13.s.s3.o.c: Because Rule 2 looks only at the high score, so it is always easier than Rule 3
z-m-37-13.s.s3.r.c: You used the feeling of 'easier' as your reason. Explain it with concrete score conditions.
z-m-37-13.s.s3.o.d: Because if both scores are below 60, the average is also below 60
z-m-37-13.s.s3.r.d: You used the contrapositive to show 'if you don't pass Rule 2, you don't pass Rule 3 either'.
z-m-37-13.s.s3.explain: If a student does not pass Rule 2, then x<60 and y<60, so x+y<120, and the student does not pass Rule 3 either. This contrapositive is the reason for Rule 3 ⊂ Rule 2.
z-m-37-13.s.s4.prompt: Design a new rule. Rule 4: the average is at least 60, and no subject is below 40. Write the inclusion relations among the sets of passers of Rule 1, Rule 3, and Rule 4, and give as an example one pair of scores that passes Rule 3 but does not pass Rule 4.
z-m-37-13.s.s4.hint.0: First judge whether Rule 4 adds to Rule 3's condition or takes from it.
z-m-37-13.s.s4.hint.1: Check whether the score range of a student who passed Rule 1 satisfies the extra condition of Rule 4.
z-m-37-13.s.s4.placeholder: Example: Rule 1 ⊂ ..., and for example ... points and ... points are ...
z-m-37-13.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Did I state the direction Rule 1 ⊂ Rule 4 ⊂ Rule 3 correctly?
z-m-37-13.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Did I explain why a Rule 1 passer passes Rule 4?
z-m-37-13.s.s4.model.0: A Rule 1 passer has an average of at least 60 and both scores are at least 40, so also passes Rule 4, so Rule 1 ⊂ Rule 4 ⊂ Rule 3. Example: 100 and 20 average 60, so it passes Rule 3, but 20 is below 40, so it does not pass Rule 4.
z-m-37-13.s.s4.model.1: Rule 4 adds one more condition to Rule 3, so Rule 4 passers also pass Rule 3, and it is narrower. A Rule 1 passer has both scores at least 60, so nothing below 40, so passes Rule 4 too. Conversely, (100, 20) passes only Rule 3.
